newsitem.title: FRANCE: LVMH nibbles at Grand Met, seeks allies - analysts.
newsitem.headline: LVMH nibbles at Grand Met, seeks allies - analysts.

text.p: France's LVMH, stung by a renewed merger pledge between British drinks companies Guinness Plc and Grand Metropolitan Plc, confirmed Tuesday that it had nudged up its stake in Grand Met to 6.3 percent.

The French luxury goods maker declined to comment on its intentions, but industry sources and analysts expect it to keep buying Grand Met shares unless the British companies agree to discuss LVMH Chairman Bernard Arnault's alternative proposal.

LVMH, the biggest shareholder in Grand Met and Guinness, opposes their plan to merge into a giant with a market worth of $33 billion with activities ranging from Haagen-Dazs ice cream to Guinness stout and Green Giant canned vegetables.

Arnault, reputed in France for his tenacity and sharp business sense, wants to create a drinks group combining LVMH's Moet & Chandon and Hennessy brands with Guinness's Johnny Walker, Dewar's and Gordon's Gin labels and possibly Grand Met's Smirnoff, J&B and Baileys brands.

If LVMH raised its Grand Met stake to 10 percent, it could call an extraordinary general meeting of Grand Met shareholders. And if it lined up enough allies to form a 25 percent block, it could stop the merger.
Most analysts say that appears to be LVMH's game plan.
"Arnault does not want to be marginalized in the drinks business," one Paris-based analyst said. He said Arnault looked to have won over a few fund managers.
LVMH, which had built its stake in Grand Met last week, bought another 250,000 shares at an average price of 587 pence ($9.57) a share, bringing its stake up to 6.3 percent, market sources said.
The next moves "depend on the reaction from Guinness and Grand Met. There are a lot of possibilities," an industry source said.

One analyst said LVMH's purchases suggested it may be less confident than it appeared on the strength of its legal case against Guinness. LVMH threatened last month to buy Guinness out of their joint distribution ventures, which hold the rights to market Guinness brands in France, the United States and much of the Far East for 10 years.
